docs.title: QIMP
docs.text:
qimp-mi is a Python library for quantum image processing on Qiskit.

It provides five image encodings (FRQI, NEQR, QPIE and the RGB extensions MCRQI and NCQI), geometric and chromatic operations, quantum Hadamard edge detection (QHED), reversible arithmetic on NEQR intensity registers, Boolean-function compression of the encoders, a variational image classifier, ratiometric image operators, simulation and IBM Quantum execution helpers, and image metrics. The standard circuit catalogue is also surveyed in C. Dolciami, "A quantum circuit library for image processing", M.Sc. thesis, Politecnico di Torino, 2022.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Every circuit is a function of the image size and bit depth. Encoders accept any n (image side 2^n), q (intensity qubits) and m (number of stacked images, multi-image FRQI). No sizes are hard-coded, and the tests are parametrised over n and q.
  • Qiskit 1.0 or later, Python 3.10 or later, src/ layout, hatchling build, ruff and strict mypy.
  • Encoding, processing, QML, I/O, runtime and testing are separate subpackages. The user interface and the IBM Quantum runtime are optional extras.

docs.title: Install

git clone https://github.com/Metabolic-Intelligence-Lab/QIMP.git
cd QIMP
pip install -e ".[dev]"

See Getting started for the optional extras.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from qimp.encoding.frqi import FrqiEncoder
from qimp.encoding.neqr import NeqrEncoder
from qimp.metrics import psnr
from qimp.testing import exact_counts, ideal_simulation

image = np.random.default_rng(0).integers(0, 256, (4, 4)).astype(np.uint8)

frqi = FrqiEncoder()
qc = frqi.encode(image)                       # 2n + 1 = 5 qubits
decoded = frqi.decode(ideal_simulation(qc, shots=40_000, seed=0))
print("FRQI PSNR:", psnr(image, decoded), "dB")

neqr = NeqrEncoder(q=8)
qc = neqr.encode(image)                       # 2n + q = 12 qubits
assert (neqr.decode(exact_counts(qc)) == image).all()

docs.title: Encodings
docs.text:
All encoders share one interface: encode(image) returns a QuantumCircuit and decode(counts) returns the image reconstructed from measurement counts. Image side 2^n and, where relevant, bit depth q are taken from the input or passed explicitly.

Encoding Class Image Qubits Retrieval FRQI FrqiEncoder grey-scale 2n + 1 statistical (shot noise) NEQR NeqrEncoder grey-scale 2n + q exact QPIE QpieEncoder grey-scale 2n statistical (shot noise) MCRQI McrqiEncoder RGB 2n + 3 statistical (shot noise) NCQI NcqiEncoder RGB 2n + 3q exact

docs.title: FRQI
docs.text:
Flexible representation of quantum images. Each pixel intensity sets the angle of a rotation of one colour qubit, controlled by the position register. The circuit is compact in qubits, and the intensity is recovered from measurement statistics.

import numpy as np
from qimp.encoding.frqi import FrqiEncoder
from qimp.testing import ideal_simulation

image = np.random.default_rng(0).integers(0, 256, (4, 4)).astype(np.uint8)
encoder = FrqiEncoder()
qc = encoder.encode(image)
recovered = encoder.decode(ideal_simulation(qc, shots=40_000, seed=0))

A stack of images of shape (num_images, H, W) adds m = ceil(log2(num_images)) selection qubits, and decode returns a list of images. Stacks whose length is not a power of two are zero-padded.

docs.title: NEQR
docs.text:
Novel enhanced quantum representation. The intensity of each pixel is written as a basis state of a q-qubit register, conditioned on the position register. Retrieval is exact, which is what the arithmetic operations need, at the cost of q extra qubits and more gates per pixel.

from qimp.encoding.neqr import NeqrEncoder
from qimp.testing import exact_counts

encoder = NeqrEncoder(q=8)
qc = encoder.encode(image)
assert (encoder.decode(exact_counts(qc)) == image).all()

docs.title: QPIE
docs.text:
Quantum probability image encoding. The normalised intensities are the amplitudes of the position register, |psi> = sum_i (I_i / ||I||) |i>. It uses the fewest qubits (2n), but the state preparation transpiles to deep circuits. The decoder rescales with the norm computed at encoding time.

from qimp.encoding.qpie import QpieEncoder

encoder = QpieEncoder()
qc = encoder.encode(image.astype(float))
recovered = encoder.decode(ideal_simulation(qc, shots=80_000, seed=0))

QHED edge detection works on QPIE states.

docs.title: MCRQI and NCQI
docs.text:
RGB extensions of FRQI and NEQR. MCRQI uses one colour qubit per channel (2n + 3 qubits); NCQI uses one q-qubit intensity register per channel (2n + 3q qubits) and retrieves the image exactly. Both take an array of shape (H, W, 3).

from qimp.encoding.ncqi import NcqiEncoder

rgb = np.random.default_rng(1).integers(0, 4, (2, 2, 3))
encoder = NcqiEncoder(q=2)
qc = encoder.encode(rgb)
assert (encoder.decode(exact_counts(qc)) == rgb).all()

docs.title: Compression
docs.text:
qimp.encoding.compression reduces the multi-controlled gates of FRQI and NEQR. The pixels that share an intensity (FRQI) or an intensity bit (NEQR) form a Boolean function of the position bits; minimising that function gives fewer, partially controlled gates. FrqiCompressor and NeqrCompressor build the compressed circuits and produce the same state as the uncompressed encoders. The cover of the function must be disjoint, because the gates act by angle sum (FRQI) or XOR (NEQR). Two minimisers are available through the method argument: exact Quine-McCluskey ("qm") and the ESPRESSO heuristic ("espresso"), which scales to larger images. The default, "auto", uses Quine-McCluskey up to n = 4 and ESPRESSO above.

from qimp.encoding.compression import NeqrCompressor

compressor = NeqrCompressor(image, q=8, method="auto")
qc = compressor.neqr_image()        # same state as NeqrEncoder(q=8).encode(image)

docs.title: Qubit layout
docs.text:
All encodings use the same position register:

Qubits Role 0 .. n-1 column index, least significant bit first n .. 2n-1 row index, least significant bit first

FRQI puts its colour qubit at 2n. NEQR puts the intensity register on qubits 0 .. q-1 and the position register above it, so geometric operations on NEQR circuits take pos_offset=q. QPIE has no extra qubits.

In a Qiskit count string, which is written most significant bit first, the leftmost position bit is the high bit of the row index and the rightmost is the low bit of the column index.

docs.title: Choosing an encoding
docs.text:
• Exact pixel values for arithmetic, comparison or sorting: NEQR (or NCQI for RGB).
  • Fewest qubits: QPIE, which is also the input of QHED.
  • One extra qubit and a rotation per pixel: FRQI (or MCRQI for RGB).

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
The public API takes the image size from the input, so the same code works for any size that fits in the simulator or on the device:

import numpy as np
from qimp.encoding.frqi import FrqiEncoder

encoder = FrqiEncoder()
qc = encoder.encode(np.zeros((16, 16), dtype=np.uint8))   # n = 4, 9 qubits
qc = encoder.encode(np.zeros((64, 64), dtype=np.uint8))   # n = 6, 13 qubits

The limit is the memory of the simulator or the qubit count and gate fidelity of the device.

docs.title: Processing
docs.text: Processing functions take a circuit and act on its registers in place. They also return the circuit, so calls can be chained.

docs.title: Geometric (qimp.processing.geometric)
docs.text:
Geometric operations act only on the position register, so they work on every encoding. pos_offset gives the first position qubit: 0 for FRQI and QPIE, q for NEQR.

Function Effect axis_flip(qc, n, axis, pos_offset=0) flip along the X or Y axis coord_swap(qc, n, pos_offset=0) transpose (swap rows and columns) ort_rotation(qc, n, angle, pos_offset=0) rotation by 90, 180 or 270 degrees pos_shift(qc, n, axis, direction="+", magnitude=1, pos_offset=0) cyclic shift restr_flip(qc, n, axis, region_bits, pos_offset=0) flip of a sub-region restr_coord_swap(qc, n, region_bits, pos_offset=0) transpose of a sub-region 
import numpy as np
from qimp.encoding.neqr import NeqrEncoder
from qimp.processing.geometric import axis_flip
from qimp.testing import exact_counts

image = np.arange(16).reshape(4, 4)
encoder = NeqrEncoder(q=4)
qc = encoder.encode(image)
axis_flip(qc, 2, axis="x", pos_offset=4)
assert (encoder.decode(exact_counts(qc)) == image[::-1, :]).all()

The tests check each operation by encoding with NEQR, applying it, decoding and comparing with the NumPy equivalent (np.flipud, np.fliplr, np.transpose, np.rot90, np.roll).

docs.title: Chromatic (qimp.processing.chromatic)
docs.text: Function Encoding Effect frqi_color_complement(qc) FRQI angle theta becomes pi/2 - theta frqi_color_change(qc, theta) FRQI rotation of all intensities by theta neqr_color_complement(qc, q) NEQR intensity I becomes 2^q - 1 - I neqr_half_intensity(qc, q) NEQR right shift of the intensity bits neqr_classify_complement(qc, q, threshold_bit) NEQR flip of the intensity bits below threshold_bit

docs.title: Edge detection (qimp.processing.filters)
docs.text:
Quantum Hadamard edge detection (QHED) on QPIE states. qhed_filter adds one auxiliary qubit, Hadamard gates and a cyclic decrement, and qhed_decode reads the intensity differences of neighbouring pixels from the counts. qhed_full_edges combines a pass on the image and a pass on its transpose.

from qimp.processing.filters import qhed_filter, qhed_full_edges
from qimp.testing import ideal_simulation

image = np.zeros((8, 8))
image[2:6, 2:6] = 1.0
qc_h, n, rms = qhed_filter(image)
qc_v, _, _ = qhed_filter(image.T)
edges = qhed_full_edges(
    image,
    ideal_simulation(qc_h, shots=40_000, seed=0),
    ideal_simulation(qc_v, shots=40_000, seed=0),
)

Wrap-around

The cyclic decrement runs over the flattened image, so the last pixel of each row is compared with the first pixel of the next row. The last column of the horizontal pass, and the last row of the vertical pass once transposed back, contain these wrap-around values and are usually discarded.

docs.title: Arithmetic (qimp.processing.arithmetic)
docs.text:
Reversible arithmetic on NEQR intensity registers. Registers are lists of qubit indices, least significant bit first. Every block has an exact inverse, so it can be uncomputed or used inside a larger algorithm.

Group Functions Addition and subtraction qc_add_1, q_add, q_sub, their inverses (_inv), controlled versions (_ctrl, _ctrl_inv) and q_add_sub_ctrl Comparison and sorting neqr_comparator, neqr_compare_swap, neqr_sort and their inverses Multiplication q_mul_const, q_mul_const_inv (by a classical constant) Division q_div_restoring, q_div_nonrestoring, q_div_general, q_div_lookup and their inverses; q_div is the default divider Synthesis synth_pixel_map, which builds any classical map between registers from its truth table

The dividers set a flag qubit on division by zero. The non-restoring divider gives the same result as the restoring one with fewer two-qubit gates.

docs.title: Ratiometric operators (qimp.processing.ratiometric_circuit)
docs.text:
Circuits that compute per-pixel ratios of two co-registered NEQR images inside the circuit, built on the arithmetic above. dual_neqr_load loads the two images on a shared position register.

Builder Decoder Result class_b_ratio decode_class_b_ratio integer ratio I_a // I_b with a divide-by-zero flag class_a_gp_prefix, class_a_gp_full decode_class_a_prefix, decode_class_a_full generalised polarisation (I_a - G I_b) / (I_a + G I_b) class_c_rogfp_full decode_class_c_rogfp calibrated redox ratio (R - R_red) / (R_ox - R_red)

The Class A builders take the G-factor as G (default 1.0), represented in fixed point as K / 2^f; gp_g_fixed_point returns (K, f), and a value that is not dyadic needs an explicit g_frac_bits. class_a_gp_lookup and class_c_rogfp_lookup build the same maps by truth-table synthesis. mark_good_oracle marks the pixels whose quotient exceeds a threshold, for use in amplitude estimation. class_b_ratio_inv, dual_neqr_load_inv and mark_good_oracle_inv uncompute the corresponding blocks.

docs.title: GP ratio by parameter synthesis (qimp.processing.gp_ratio)
docs.text: A variational route to the Laurdan GP image on FRQI states: classical_gp_image is the NumPy reference, analytical_gp_params gives closed-form parameters, apply_gp_function adds the parametrised sub-circuit, and optimize_gp fits the parameters with a weighted objective of MSE, PSNR and total variation (combined_objective).

docs.title: Classification (qimp.qml.classifier)
docs.text:
FrqiClassifier is a binary variational classifier: a RealAmplitudes ansatz on the FRQI state, read out as the expectation of Z on the colour qubit, trained with COBYLA on labels -1 and +1.

from qimp.qml.classifier import FrqiClassifier

clf = FrqiClassifier(reps=1, seed=0)
dark, bright = np.zeros((2, 2)), np.ones((2, 2))
clf.fit([dark, bright], [-1, 1], max_iter=20)
clf.predict([dark, bright])

docs.title: Simulation (qimp.testing)
docs.text:
Function Use exact_counts(qc) noise-free counts computed from the statevector, without sampling; used by the tests ideal_simulation(qc, shots, seed=None) shot sampling on the noise-free Aer simulator; seed makes it reproducible noisy_simulation(qc, shots, noise_model=None) shot sampling with an Aer noise model device_test(qc, shots, backend_name=None) execution on an IBM Quantum backend (needs the [ibm] extra)

Measurements are added when the circuit has none. qimp.runtime.get_simulator returns a shared AerSimulator and uses the GPU when qiskit-aer-gpu is installed.

docs.title: IBM Quantum (qimp.runtime.ibm)
docs.text:
The module needs the [ibm] extra and an API token saved with QiskitRuntimeService.save_account(...).

from qimp.runtime.ibm import get_service, hw_run, pick_backend

service = get_service()
backend = pick_backend(service, min_qubits=qc.num_qubits)   # least busy
counts, transpiled, job_id, summary = hw_run(
    qc, backend=backend, shots=4096, mitigation="trex+dd"
)

hw_run transpiles the circuit for the backend and submits it with the SamplerV2 primitive. The mitigation argument selects:

Value Effect "trex+dd" (default) measurement twirling (TREX) and dynamical decoupling "trex" measurement twirling only "dd" dynamical decoupling only (dd_sequence, default "XY4") "zne" zero-noise extrapolation on top of TREX and dynamical decoupling "none" no mitigation

summary holds the depth, gate counts and options of the run, and persist_run saves the circuit (QPY), counts and metadata to disk. aer_noisy_run runs the same circuit on Aer with the noise model of a backend, without using QPU time.

docs.title: Zero-noise extrapolation (qimp.runtime.zne)
docs.text:
The sampler returns counts, not expectation values, so zero-noise extrapolation is done on the counts:

  1. fold_gates(qc, scale) amplifies the gate noise by global folding, U (U^dag U)^k, after transpilation, with barriers so that the folds are not optimised away. Fractional scales fold a final part of the circuit once more. Measurements are kept.
  2. The folded circuits for the scales (default 1, 3, 5) are submitted in one job.
  3. zne_probabilities and zne_extrapolate extrapolate the probability of each bitstring to zero noise with a polynomial through all points ("richardson"), a least-squares line ("linear") or a global depolarising decay ("exponential"), then clip to [0, 1] and renormalise.
counts, transpiled, job_id, summary = hw_run(
    qc, backend=backend, mitigation="zne", zne_scales=(1, 3, 5), zne_method="linear"
)
summary["zne_raw_counts"]   # counts at each scale, to redo the fit offline

The same extrapolation can be tested without an IBM account:

from qiskit.providers.fake_provider import GenericBackendV2
from qimp.runtime.ibm import aer_noisy_run

counts = aer_noisy_run(qc, backend=GenericBackendV2(5), zne_scales=(1, 3, 5), seed=0)

Folding amplifies gate errors but not readout errors, which TREX handles. Richardson extrapolation amplifies shot noise; on hardware the linear fit is usually more stable.

docs.title: Hardware sweep
docs.text: scripts/run_hardware_sweep.py runs every encoder at several sizes on the ideal simulator, on Aer with a backend noise model and optionally on hardware, and writes a summary table, figures and the raw runs to data/output/ibm/<UTC-timestamp>/. See the README for the command-line options.

docs.title: Interactive UI
docs.text: The QIMP Explorer is a Streamlit application for running the encoders, the processing operations and the GP-ratio pipeline without writing code.

docs.title: Install and launch
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[ui]"        # adds streamlit and pandas
pip install -e ".[ui,ibm]"    # also needed to submit circuits to IBM Quantum
qimp ui                       # or: streamlit run apps/qimp_explorer/app.py

The application opens at http://localhost:8501.

docs.title: Main page
docs.text:
The main page has five steps, each enabled once the previous one is done:

  1. Load: upload a TIFF or PNG file, or pick one from data/immagini/.
  2. Preprocess: resize to a power-of-two side (2 to 64 pixels) and optionally convert RGB to grey scale (BT.601 luma).
  3. Encode: choose FRQI, NEQR, QPIE, MCRQI or NCQI and the intensity qubits where relevant. The step reports the qubit count and the depth before and after transpilation.
  4. Process (optional): apply geometric operations (flip, swap, rotation) and chromatic operations (colour complement, half intensity). After each operation an 8192-shot ideal simulation shows the image before and after. "Reset ops" restores the encoded circuit.
  5. Execute and export: run the circuit on the ideal or noisy simulator, copy it as OpenQASM 3, or submit it to an IBM Quantum backend through the Sampler primitive. The API token is entered in the sidebar and kept only in the session.

Saved outputs are written as TIFF files to data/output/run_<timestamp>/.

docs.title: Other pages
docs.text: Page Content Benchmark FRQI, NEQR and QPIE on the same image, with a table of PSNR, total variation, depth and run time, and bar charts GP-ratio classical GP image in three output formats (normalised, uint8, 16-bit), optional Gaussian and median filtering, and construction of the parametric circuit System Info library, Qiskit and Python versions, simulator backend and GPU detection, dataset statistics, previous runs, cache clearing

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• FRQI circuits grow quickly above n = 3 because of the multi-controlled rotations. Resize to 4x4 or 8x8 in the Preprocess step.
  • NEQR recovers the image exactly.
  • The GP-ratio page builds the parametric circuit and reports its depth and gate counts but does not run the optimisation, which takes more than ten minutes per image on a CPU simulator. Use qimp.processing.gp_ratio.optimize_gp in a script for that.

docs.title: qimp.encoding.frqi
docs.text:
FRQI encoding: Flexible Representation of Quantum Images.

A 2^n × 2^n grayscale image is encoded into 2n+1 qubits: 2n position qubits plus 1 color qubit. The pixel intensity is mapped to an RY rotation angle and applied via a fully-controlled RY gate. Multiple images can be stacked by adding m = ceil(log2(num_images)) selection qubits, for a total of 2n+m+1 qubits.

Scales freely with n (image side = 2^n) and m (number of stacked images = 2^m).

Reference: P.Q. Le, F. Dong, K. Hirota, Quantum Inf. Process. 10 (2011) 63-84.

docs.title: FrqiEncoder
docs.text:
Stateful FRQI encoder.

Bundles the normalization factor and inferred n/m so the same instance can be reused for encode→measure→decode round-trips.

docs.title: intensities_to_angles
docs.text:
intensities_to_angles(intensities: ndarray, normalization: float) -> np.ndarray

Map pixel intensities to RY angles in [0, π].

Convention: intensity 0 → θ = 0, intensity = normalization → θ = π. After RY(θ), prob(color qubit = 1) = sin²(θ/2) = intensity / normalization.

docs.title: angles_to_intensities
docs.text:
angles_to_intensities(angles: ndarray, normalization: float) -> np.ndarray

Inverse of intensities_to_angles.

docs.title: frqi_circuit
docs.text:
frqi_circuit(images: ndarray | Sequence[ndarray], *, normalization: float | None = None) -> QuantumCircuit

Build an FRQI quantum circuit for one or more square images.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default images ndarray | Sequence[ndarray]

A single 2D image (shape (2^n, 2^n)), a 3D stack (shape (num_images, 2^n, 2^n)), or a sequence of 2D images. When more than one image is supplied, num_images is padded with zero images to the next power of two and m = log2(num_images_padded) selection qubits are added.

required normalization float | None

Intensity that maps to angle π (full color amplitude on |1⟩). Defaults to the max value of the dtype (255 for uint8, 65535 for uint16, 1.0 for float).

None

Returns:

Type Description QuantumCircuit

Circuit with 2n + m + 1 qubits and an equal number of classical bits. No measurement gates are appended; call ideal_simulation / device_test on the returned circuit (they add measurements automatically).

docs.title: frqi_decode
docs.text:
frqi_decode(counts: dict[str, int], n: int, m: int = 0, normalization: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray | list[np.ndarray]

Decode measurement counts from an FRQI circuit into one or more images.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default counts dict[str, int]

Qiskit-style histogram from ideal_simulation(qc, shots).

required n int

Number of spatial qubits per axis (image side = 2^n).

required m int

Number of selection qubits (number of images = 2^m). Defaults to 0 (single image).

0 normalization float

Intensity that maps to θ = π — must match what was used at encoding. The reconstructed intensity for pixel j of image s is prob(color=1 | pos=j, sel=s) * normalization.

1.0

Returns:

Type Description ndarray | list[ndarray]
  • When m == 0 (single image): a single (2^n, 2^n) float array, matching the shape contract of neqr_decode / qpie_decode.
  • When m > 0: a list of 2^m images, since only FRQI supports multi-image encoding via image-selection qubits.

docs.title: qimp.encoding.neqr
docs.text:
NEQR encoding: Novel Enhanced Quantum Representation.

A 2^n × 2^n grayscale image with intensity resolution 2^q is encoded into 2n + q qubits. The intensity is stored in a separate q-bit register (basis-state encoding), enabling exact retrieval and arithmetic operations.

Qubit layout (low → high index): - q intensity qubits (qubits 0 … q-1) - n X-position qubits (qubits q … q+n-1) - n Y-position qubits (qubits q+n … q+2n-1)

Reference: Y. Zhang et al., Quantum Inf. Process. 12 (2013) 2833-2860.

docs.title: NeqrEncoder
docs.text: Stateful NEQR encoder that records n and q for round-trips.

docs.title: neqr_circuit
docs.text:
neqr_circuit(image: ndarray, q: int = 8) -> QuantumCircuit

Build a NEQR circuit for a single grayscale image.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default image ndarray

Square (2^n, 2^n) integer array with values in [0, 2^q - 1].

required q int

Number of intensity qubits. Image values must fit in q bits.

8

Returns:

Type Description QuantumCircuit

Circuit with 2n + q qubits.

Notes

Complexity: O(q · n · 2^(2n)) gates worst-case. Scales freely with both n and q.

docs.title: neqr_decode
docs.text:
neqr_decode(counts: dict[str, int], n: int, q: int) -> np.ndarray

Decode NEQR measurement counts into the reconstructed image.

For each position, the most-frequent intensity reading is taken (NEQR is exact, so ideal simulations yield a single intensity per pixel).

docs.title: qimp.encoding.qpie
docs.text:
QPIE encoding: Quantum Probability Image Encoding.

Pixel intensities are normalized so that their squared values sum to 1, then loaded as amplitude probabilities into 2n qubits via Qiskit's initialize. Compact (only 2n qubits) but produces an arbitrary state preparation that transpiles to deep circuits.

Reference: X.-W. Yao et al., Phys. Rev. X 7 (2017) 031041.

docs.title: QpieEncoder
docs.text: Stateful QPIE encoder that records n and the RMS for decoding.

docs.text:
qpie_circuit(image: ndarray) -> QuantumCircuit

Build a QPIE circuit for a single grayscale image.

The circuit has 2n qubits; the state is |Ψ⟩ = Σ_i (I_i / ‖I‖) |i⟩ where |i⟩ is the position basis state.

Scales freely with n. The intensity resolution is bounded only by the number of measurement shots (no q parameter — QPIE has no intensity register).

docs.title: qimp.encoding.mcrqi
docs.text:
MCRQI encoding: FRQI extension to RGB images.

A 2^n × 2^n RGB image is encoded into 2n + 3 qubits: 2n position qubits and 3 color qubits (one per channel R / G / B). Each color qubit independently carries the channel's pixel intensity as an RY rotation angle.

Compared to FRQI: - adds 2 qubits (3 color qubits instead of 1); - per-pixel construction is 3 fully-controlled RY gates instead of 1.

Reference: B. Sun et al., J. Adv. Comput. Intell. Intell. Inform. 17 (2013) 404-417.

docs.title: qimp.encoding.ncqi
docs.text:
NCQI encoding: NEQR extension to RGB images.

A 2^n × 2^n RGB image with intensity resolution 2^q per channel is encoded into 2n + 3q qubits. The intensity of each channel sits in its own q-bit basis-state register; retrieval is exact.

Qubit layout (low → high index): - q R-intensity qubits (qubits 0 … q-1) - q G-intensity qubits (qubits q … 2q-1) - q B-intensity qubits (qubits 2q … 3q-1) - n X-position qubits (qubits 3q … 3q+n-1) - n Y-position qubits (qubits 3q+n … 3q+2n-1)

Reference: J. Sang, S. Wang, Q. Li, Quantum Inf. Process. 16 (2017) 42.

docs.title: qimp.encoding.compression
docs.text:
FRQI / NEQR compression via Boolean-function minimisation.

Pixels that share the same intensity (FRQI) or the same intensity-bit (NEQR) form a Boolean function of the position bits. Minimising that function shrinks the number of control patterns needed, which reduces the per-pixel multi-controlled gates issued by the encoder.

Two self-contained minimisers are provided, with no extra dependency:

  • Quine–McCluskey (compress_minterms) followed by a greedy disjoint cover. Used by default for small position registers.
  • An ESPRESSO-style heuristic (espresso_minimize: EXPAND / IRREDUNDANT / REDUCE on cube covers) followed by make_disjoint_cover. Used by default for 2n >= ESPRESSO_AUTO_MIN_WIDTH (n >= 5), where enumerating all prime implicants becomes expensive.

Both paths return a disjoint cover that reproduces the on-set exactly, which the encoders require. Select the path with method="auto" | "qm" | "espresso" on FrqiCompressor, NeqrCompressor or position_strings_to_implicants.

References
  • W. V. Quine, "The problem of simplifying truth functions", Amer. Math. Monthly 59 (1952); E. J. McCluskey, "Minimization of Boolean functions", Bell Syst. Tech. J. 35 (1956).
  • R. K. Brayton, G. D. Hachtel, C. T. McMullen, A. L. Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, "Logic Minimization Algorithms for VLSI Synthesis", Kluwer (1984).

docs.title: compress_minterms
docs.text:
compress_minterms(minterms: Iterable[str]) -> list[str]

Return prime implicants for a Boolean function given by minterms.

Each input is a fixed-width binary string. Output strings use "-" for don't-cares. The set returned covers every minterm in minterms (no further essential-prime-implicant selection — the result is a cover, not necessarily the smallest one).

For typical FRQI/NEQR uses (n ≤ 4) this is fast and correct. For larger fan-ins use espresso_minimize.

docs.title: espresso_minimize
docs.text:
espresso_minimize(minterms: Iterable[str], dont_cares: Iterable[str] = ()) -> list[str]

Heuristic two-level minimisation of a single-output Boolean function.

Pure-Python ESPRESSO-style loop: the on-set is expanded into prime cubes against the off-set (EXPAND), redundant cubes are removed (IRREDUNDANT), then the cover is repeatedly reduced (REDUCE), re-expanded and made irredundant until the cost (number of cubes, then number of literals) stops decreasing.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default minterms Iterable[str]

On-set, as fixed-width strings over "0", "1" (and optionally "-", so cubes are accepted too). MSB first.

required dont_cares Iterable[str]

Optional DC-set in the same format. The result may cover any part of it.

()

Returns:

Type Description list[str]

Sorted implicant strings. Their union contains the on-set and is contained in on-set plus DC-set. The cubes are prime and irredundant but may overlap; see make_disjoint_cover for an exact partition. The cover is not guaranteed to be minimum.

docs.title: make_disjoint_cover
docs.text:
make_disjoint_cover(cover: Iterable[str]) -> list[str]

Rewrite a cover as pairwise disjoint implicants with the same union.

Cubes are taken largest first; each new cube is cut by disjoint sharp against every cube already placed, then adjacent pieces are merged. Every output cube contains at least one minterm, so the result never has more cubes than the function has minterms.

docs.title: position_strings_to_implicants
docs.text:
position_strings_to_implicants(positions: Iterable[int], width: int, *, method: CompressionMethod = 'auto') -> list[str]

Pixel indices → disjoint cover of width-bit implicants.

With method="qm", runs Quine–McCluskey to find prime implicants, then greedy set-partitioning to ensure the returned implicants do not overlap on any minterm. With method="espresso", runs espresso_minimize and then make_disjoint_cover. method="auto" uses Quine–McCluskey for width < ESPRESSO_AUTO_MIN_WIDTH and ESPRESSO otherwise.

Either way the result covers each given position exactly once and no other position, so it can be turned directly into a sequence of multi-controlled gates.

docs.title: qimp.processing.geometric
docs.text:
Geometric transformations on encoded quantum images.

These operations manipulate position qubits only and therefore apply identically to FRQI, NEQR, and QPIE. The caller supplies n (qubits per spatial axis) and an offset that points to the first position qubit in the target circuit:

============ ================================= Encoding Position-qubit offset ============ ================================= FRQI 0 (qubits 0..2n-1) QPIE 0 (qubits 0..2n-1) NEQR q (qubits q..q+2n-1, with q the intensity-qubit count) ============ =================================

Qubit layout within the position block (LSB-first): - pos_offset .. pos_offset + n - 1 → X-axis qubits (column, x_0 … x_{n-1}) - pos_offset + n .. pos_offset + 2n - 1 → Y-axis qubits (row, y_0 … y_{n-1})

docs.title: axis_flip
docs.text:
axis_flip(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, axis: Axis, *, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Flip the image about the given axis.

axis='x' flips about the X axis (inverts Y / row coordinate) by applying X gates to the Y-axis qubits. axis='y' flips about the Y axis (inverts X / column coordinate) by applying X gates to the X-axis qubits.

Complexity: O(n) X gates.

docs.title: coord_swap
docs.text:
coord_swap(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, *, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Swap row and column coordinates: image transpose.

Applies n SWAP gates between paired position qubits (x_i, y_i). Complexity: O(n) SWAPs ≡ 3n CNOTs.

docs.title: ort_rotation
docs.text:
ort_rotation(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, angle: int, *, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Rotate the image by 90°, 180°, or 270° counter-clockwise.

Decomposition into flip + swap:

  • 90°: coord_swap then axis_flip('y') (swap rows/cols, then invert cols)
  • 180°: axis_flip('x') then axis_flip('y')
  • 270°: coord_swap then axis_flip('x')

docs.title: pos_shift
docs.text:
pos_shift(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, axis: Axis, *, direction: Literal['+', '-'] = '+', magnitude: int = 1, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Shift the image by magnitude pixels along axis.

Implemented as a cyclic increment / decrement on the n-qubit position register for that axis. Each cyclic step is a cascade of multi-controlled X gates of decreasing arity (Toffoli-tower), giving O(n²) gate complexity.

docs.title: restr_flip
docs.text:
restr_flip(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, axis: Axis, region_bits: str, *, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Flip only the pixels whose position prefix matches region_bits.

Each character of region_bits selects a higher-order qubit of the axis being preserved (the axis not being flipped). For example, with n=4 and region_bits="10" on axis='y': flip the column coordinate only for rows whose two MSBs are 10 (i.e. rows 8..11).

Implemented as a multi-controlled X on each X-axis qubit, with controls on the higher-order qubits of the orthogonal axis taking the prefix as a bitmask.

docs.title: restr_coord_swap
docs.text:
restr_coord_swap(qc: QuantumCircuit, n: int, region_bits: str, *, pos_offset: int = 0) -> QuantumCircuit

Coord-swap restricted to a region selected by region_bits.

Decomposition idea: for each i, apply a controlled-SWAP between x_i and y_i conditioned on the region prefix. Implemented as CSWAP = CNOT(b,a) → Toffoli(ctrl..., a, b) → CNOT(b, a) per pair.

frqi_color_complement(qc: QuantumCircuit, *, color_qubit: int | None = None) -> QuantumCircuit

Invert FRQI colors by applying an X to the color qubit.

Maps cos(θ)|0⟩ + sin(θ)|1⟩ → sin(θ)|0⟩ + cos(θ)|1⟩, i.e. θ → π/2 − θ. If color_qubit is None the highest-indexed qubit is used.

frqi_color_change(qc: QuantumCircuit, theta: float, *, color_qubit: int | None = None) -> QuantumCircuit

Apply a custom unitary on the FRQI color qubit, parameterised by theta.

The unitary is [[cos(θ/2), sin(θ/2)], [sin(θ/2), -cos(θ/2)]] — a reflection matrix that maps cos(α)|0⟩ + sin(α)|1⟩ → cos(α+θ)|0⟩ + sin(α+θ)|1⟩, shifting every pixel intensity by θ modulo π.

docs.title: neqr_color_complement

neqr_color_complement(qc: QuantumCircuit, q: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Bit-wise NOT of every intensity bit: maps i → (2^q − 1) − i for each pixel.

Applies an X gate to each of the q intensity qubits (assumed to be the lowest-indexed q qubits, per the NEQR layout).

docs.title: neqr_half_intensity
docs.text:
neqr_half_intensity(qc: QuantumCircuit, q: int, *, allow_reset: bool = False) -> QuantumCircuit

Divide every pixel intensity by 2 (integer division) by right-shifting one bit.

Implemented as a cascade of SWAPs that re-labels intensity qubits and a final reset of the freed top bit. Effectively maps b_{q-1}…b_1 b_0 → 0 b_{q-1}…b_1.

Hardware note

The final qc.reset(q-1) is non-unitary: on a real device it implies a mid-circuit measurement + conditional X, which is not supported on many IBM backends and breaks composability with downstream unitary operations.

Pass allow_reset=True to acknowledge this and produce the textbook circuit. The default (allow_reset=False) raises rather than silently emitting a non-unitary op; use the SWAP-only cascade if you intend to run on hardware — the freed top bit will then carry whatever was there before the call (garbage if not pre-zeroed, but the circuit stays unitary).

Superposition caveat

After the SWAP cascade, qubit q-1 holds the original LSB of the intensity register, which is generally entangled with the position register on a real image. qc.reset(q-1) then projects that qubit onto |0⟩, which drops the pixel branches where the original LSB was 1. The textbook i → i // 2 map therefore only holds exactly for images with all-even intensities; on arbitrary images, half-intensity must be implemented via mid-circuit measurement + classical-conditional X (post-selection on the LSB), which the current implementation does not provide.

docs.title: qimp.processing.filters
docs.text:
Quantum filters for spatial processing.

Currently exposes the Quantum Hadamard Edge Detection (QHED) algorithm for images encoded with QPIE. QHED is a poly(n) algorithm that uses a single auxiliary qubit, a Hadamard gate, and a cyclic decrement gate to extract gradient information from adjacent pixels in a single shot batch.

Reference: X.-W. Yao et al., Phys. Rev. X 7 (2017) 031041.

docs.title: qhed_filter
docs.text:
qhed_filter(image: ndarray) -> tuple[QuantumCircuit, int, float]

Build a QHED circuit that exposes adjacent-pixel gradients of image.

The circuit has 2n + 1 qubits:

  • qubit 0: auxiliary qubit (LSB)
  • qubits 1..2n: position register holding the QPIE-encoded image

After execution, measuring with aux = 1 at position i gives a magnitude proportional to |c_i − c_{i+1}| where c are the QPIE amplitudes in row-major flattened order.

.. warning:: This is not a pure horizontal-only gradient. The cyclic decrement acts on the full register modulo 2^{2n+1}, so adjacency wraps around at every row boundary: pixel (r, 2^n − 1) is adjacent to pixel (r + 1, 0) in the flattened representation. The output therefore contains spurious "edges" at the last column of every row, which reflect the wrap-around, not the image. For a pure horizontal-only filter, transpose the image and run QHED on the transposed version, then compose horizontally / vertically yourself and discard the boundary columns.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default image ndarray

Square (2^n, 2^n) non-negative intensity array.

required

Returns:

Type Description qc

The QHED circuit (no measurements appended).

n

Spatial qubits per axis.

rms

Root-mean-square of the input intensities, √(mean(I²)). Forward this to qhed_decode to recover the absolute gradient scale.

Notes

Complexity is O(poly(n)) after Hadamard + Toffoli decomposition, excluding the QPIE initialize which dominates and is itself O(2^{2n}) in depth.

docs.title: qimp.processing.arithmetic
docs.text:
Quantum arithmetic primitives for NEQR-encoded images.

Public ops: - qc_add_1(qc, a, b, c_out) — one-bit full adder b ← (a + b) with carry-out qubit c_out. - q_add(qc, a_qubits, b_qubits, c_qubits) — ripple-carry adder b ← (a + b) for arbitrary-width little-endian registers, using one auxiliary qubit per bit (len(c_qubits) == len(a_qubits) + 1). - q_add_inv(qc, …) — exact inverse of q_add; restores carry register. - q_add_ctrl(qc, ctrl, …) — controlled adder b ← b + (ctrl ? a : 0). - q_sub(qc, a_qubits, b_qubits, c_qubits) — wrap of q_add with the two's-complement of a: b ← b - a. - q_sub_inv(qc, …) — exact inverse of q_sub. - q_mul_const(qc, b_qubits, k_bits, accum_qubits, c_qubits) — multiply b by a classical constant (bit pattern k_bits) into the accumulator via shift-add. - q_div_restoring(qc, …) — fixed-point unsigned restoring division. - neqr_comparator(qc, a_qubits, b_qubits, c_qubits, gt_qubit) — sets gt_qubit = 1 iff a > b. - neqr_compare_swap(qc, a_qubits, b_qubits, c_qubits, flag_qubit) - reversible compare-and-swap: leaves min(a, b) in a and max(a, b) in b, recording the swap decision in flag_qubit. - neqr_sort(qc, registers, c_qubits, flag_qubits) - odd-even transposition sorting network over k intensity registers.

Conventions

All registers are little-endian lists of qubit indices ([lsb, …, msb]). q_add follows the standard ripple-carry construction with one carry qubit per input bit plus one final-out qubit (so len(c_qubits) = n + 1).

Position-register independence

Every primitive in this module acts only on the explicit qubit-index lists passed in. None of them touches the NEQR position register, so they all compose uniformly across a position-superposition: if the position register holds Σ_p |p⟩ and the intensity register holds |I(p)⟩ for the addressed pixel, the primitives apply the same arithmetic transformation on |I(p)⟩ for every p in the superposition.

docs.title: qc_add_1
docs.text:
qc_add_1(qc: QuantumCircuit, a: int, b: int, c_in: int, c_out: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Single-bit full adder: b ← a ⊕ b ⊕ c_in, c_out ← MAJ(a, b, c_in).

a and c_in are read; b is overwritten with the new sum bit; c_out is set to the new carry.

docs.title: q_add
docs.text:
q_add(qc: QuantumCircuit, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int]) -> QuantumCircuit

Ripple-carry adder: b ← (a + b) mod 2^(n+1).

c_qubits provides the n+1 carry qubits (initially expected to be |0⟩; end state holds the final carry chain in c_qubits[-1]).

Complexity: O(n) full-adder stages.

docs.title: q_sub
docs.text:
q_sub(qc: QuantumCircuit, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int]) -> QuantumCircuit

Subtractor via two's-complement: b ← (b - a) mod 2^(n+1).

Implemented as b ← b + (~a + 1) using the same q_add plumbing. On exit:

  • a_qubits are restored to their input state (bitwise-NOT reversed).
  • c_qubits[0] is restored to |0⟩ (the +1 preload is uncomputed).
  • c_qubits[1..n] hold the carry chain produced by the addition; c_qubits[-1] is the final borrow bit (used by neqr_comparator).

docs.title: neqr_comparator
docs.text:
neqr_comparator(qc: QuantumCircuit, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int], gt_qubit: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Set gt_qubit = 1 iff a > b.

Implementation: compute b - a via q_sub into the b/c registers; the final carry-out (c_qubits[-1]) is 1 iff b ≥ a; we use a CNOT to write the negation into gt_qubit, and an X to flip equality to strict-greater. The caller is responsible for uncomputing b / c if they need the original b.

docs.title: qc_add_1_inv
docs.text:
qc_add_1_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, a: int, b: int, c_in: int, c_out: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Inverse of :func:qc_add_1: gates in reverse order.

docs.title: q_add_inv
docs.text:
q_add_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int]) -> QuantumCircuit

Inverse of :func:q_add: b ← (b - a) mod 2^(n+1), restoring the carry chain in c_qubits to |0⟩ (assuming it was |0⟩ going into the matching :func:q_add).

docs.title: q_sub_inv
docs.text:
q_sub_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int]) -> QuantumCircuit

Inverse of :func:q_sub: b ← (b + a) plus carry-register cleanup.

Reverses the gate sequence of q_sub: undo the +1 preload uncompute, undo the ~a bitflip, undo the addition, undo the +1 preload, undo ~a.

docs.title: qc_add_1_ctrl
docs.text:
qc_add_1_ctrl(qc: QuantumCircuit, ctrl: int, a: int, b: int, c_in: int, c_out: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Controlled single-bit full adder: applies :func:qc_add_1 on (a, b, c_in, c_out) if ctrl == 1, identity otherwise.

Each gate in qc_add_1 acquires one extra control on ctrl:

  • ccx(a, b, c_out) → mcx([ctrl, a, b], c_out)
  • cx(a, b) → ccx(ctrl, a, b)
  • ccx(b, c_in, c_out) → mcx([ctrl, b, c_in], c_out)
  • cx(c_in, b) → ccx(ctrl, c_in, b)

docs.text:
q_add_ctrl(qc: QuantumCircuit, ctrl: int, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int]) -> QuantumCircuit

Controlled ripple-carry adder: b ← (a + b) if ctrl == 1, identity otherwise. Same register-width invariants as :func:q_add.

docs.title: qc_add_1_ctrl_inv
docs.text:
qc_add_1_ctrl_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, ctrl: int, a: int, b: int, c_in: int, c_out: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Inverse of :func:qc_add_1_ctrl: same gates in reverse order (every gate is self-inverse).

docs.title: q_add_ctrl_inv
docs.text:
q_add_ctrl_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, ctrl: int, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int]) -> QuantumCircuit

Inverse of :func:q_add_ctrl: iterates in reverse order and applies :func:qc_add_1_ctrl_inv per bit.

Restores b to its pre-call value when ctrl == 1 (was b + a, now back to b) and the carry register to its pre-call state (assumed |0⟩ originally).

docs.title: q_mul_const
docs.text:
q_mul_const(qc: QuantumCircuit, b_qubits: Sequence[int], k_bits: Sequence[int], accum_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int], guard_qubit: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Multiply b by a classical constant via shift-add into a zeroed accumulator: accum ← b · k (mod 2**(q + m)).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default b_qubits Sequence[int]

q-bit input register (little-endian); preserved on exit.

required k_bits Sequence[int]

Classical bit pattern of k as a sequence of {0, 1} values, little-endian (k = Σ k_bits[i] · 2**i). len(k_bits) = m.

required accum_qubits Sequence[int]

Accumulator register of width q + m bits, |0⟩ on entry. Each set bit i of k adds b into the (q + 1)-bit window accum[i .. i + q]; starting from zero, the partial sum in that window is below 2**q before every add, so no carry is lost and the result is exactly b · k. With a non-zero accumulator on entry an intermediate add can overflow its window, and the carry-out is not propagated, so the result is not accum + b · k in general. To add a product onto an existing value, multiply into a fresh zeroed register and add it with :func:q_add.

required c_qubits Sequence[int]

Carry-scratch register. Width must be at least popcount(k) * (q + 2) — each shift consumes a fresh (q + 2)-bit slice (one more than a plain q-bit add to accommodate the zero-extended high bit of b). The slices stay dirty (entangled with the result) and must be uncomputed by running :func:q_mul_const_inv at the pipeline tail.

required guard_qubit int

A single ancilla qubit that must be |0⟩ on entry. It is used as the (zero-valued) high bit of b for each shifted add so the carry-out propagates one position up into the accumulator rather than being trapped in the carry register. It is restored to |0⟩ on exit (the all-XOR structure of q_add flips it back to its input value).

Because the guard qubit returns to |0⟩ after each call, the SAME guard qubit may be reused across multiple :func:q_mul_const calls in the same circuit — for instance in a Class-A GP pipeline where you multiply I_b by G and then later multiply by 1/(R_ox - R_red) for a Class-C reparametrisation. Allocating one guard for the whole pipeline is the recommended pattern.

required Notes

Cost: popcount(k) calls to q_add of width q + 1. The carry qubits and accumulator are entangled with each other; only :func:q_mul_const_inv cleans the whole construction.

docs.text:
q_mul_const_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, b_qubits: Sequence[int], k_bits: Sequence[int], accum_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int], guard_qubit: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Exact inverse of :func:q_mul_const.

docs.title: q_sub_ctrl
docs.text:
q_sub_ctrl(qc: QuantumCircuit, ctrl: int, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int]) -> QuantumCircuit

Controlled subtractor: b ← (b - a) if ctrl == 1, identity otherwise.

Implementation: same two's-complement trick as :func:q_sub, but every gate that mutates state is conditioned on ctrl. The bit-flip steps on a are made conditional via CNOTs so the inversion is undone whether or not the body fires.

docs.title: q_sub_ctrl_inv
docs.text:
q_sub_ctrl_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, ctrl: int, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int]) -> QuantumCircuit

Inverse of :func:q_sub_ctrl: reverses the gate order. All constituent CNOTs are self-inverse; the embedded :func:q_add_ctrl is undone by :func:q_add_ctrl_inv.

When ctrl == 1 on entry, restores b from b − a to b, and the carry register to |0⟩ (assumed |0⟩ originally). Identity when ctrl == 0.

docs.title: q_add_sub_ctrl
docs.text:
q_add_sub_ctrl(qc: QuantumCircuit, ctrl: int, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int]) -> QuantumCircuit

Controlled add-or-subtract: b ← b + a if ctrl == 0, b ← b − a if ctrl == 1.

Implementation: a single :func:q_add body, sandwiched between conditional two's-complement of a (CNOTs from ctrl to each bit of a plus a CNOT into c_qubits[0] for the +1 preload). When ctrl = 0 both sandwich layers are identity and the body computes b + a; when ctrl = 1 the body computes b + (~a + 1) = b − a.

This primitive is the workhorse of :func:q_div_nonrestoring: each iteration of non-restoring division applies one q_add_sub_ctrl instead of restoring's trial-subtract / undo / conditional-subtract trio.

docs.title: q_add_sub_ctrl_inv
docs.text:
q_add_sub_ctrl_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, ctrl: int, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int]) -> QuantumCircuit

Inverse of :func:q_add_sub_ctrl: gates in reverse, body undone by :func:q_add_inv. Restores b to its pre-call value and the carry chain to |0⟩ (assumed |0⟩ originally).

docs.title: q_div_restoring
docs.text:
q_div_restoring(qc: QuantumCircuit, dividend_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_qubits: Sequence[int], quotient_qubits: Sequence[int], work_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_pad_qubit: int, c_qubits: Sequence[int], div_zero_flag: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Unsigned fixed-point restoring division.

Computes quotient = dividend // divisor and overwrites the dividend register with the remainder dividend mod divisor.

Layout (all little-endian, width q unless stated): - dividend_qubits (q) → on exit: remainder. - divisor_qubits (q) → preserved. - quotient_qubits (q) → |0⟩ on entry, quotient on exit. - work_qubits (q) → |0⟩ on entry, restored to |0⟩ on exit (high half of the conceptual 2q-bit running register R = work || dividend). - divisor_pad_qubit (1) → ancilla, |0⟩ on entry and exit; zero-pad MSB of the divisor. - c_qubits → carry-scratch, width ≥ (q + 1) * (q + 2). Layout: first (q + 2) qubits are a shared clean slice reused by every iteration's GTE comparator; the remaining q * (q + 2) are dirty per-iteration slices for the conditional subtract (cleaned only by :func:q_div_restoring_inv). - div_zero_flag (1) → set to 1 iff divisor == 0 on entry.

Algorithm (slim-carry variant): For i in q-1 down to 0: window = R[i .. i+q] (q+1 bits) # GTE comparator (clean): trial-subtract then undo, copying the # no-borrow sign bit into quotient[i]. q_sub(D, window, c_cmp) CNOT(c_cmp[-1], quotient[i]) q_sub_inv(D, window, c_cmp) # restores window and c_cmp. # Actual conditional subtract: only fires when quotient[i] = 1. q_sub_ctrl(quotient[i], D, window, c_act_i)

Cost: q iterations × (one full q_sub-pair + one q_sub_ctrl) ≈ O(q²) Toffolis with constant factor ~10. Ancilla: (q + 1)(q + 2) carry + 1 divisor-pad.

Composition note: on exit the per-iteration c_act slices are left entangled with the quotient and remainder. This is harmless for measurement-and-discard use, where the result is read out and the carry register is thrown away. To reuse the carry register, or to embed the divider in a QAE-style oracle, follow it with :func:q_div_restoring_inv (built on :func:q_sub_ctrl_inv), which returns every ancilla to |0⟩.

docs.title: q_div_general
docs.text:
q_div_general(qc: QuantumCircuit, dividend_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_qubits: Sequence[int], quotient_qubits: Sequence[int], work_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_pad_qubit: int, c_qubits: Sequence[int], div_zero_flag: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Generalised restoring divider supporting non-square widths.

Computes quotient = dividend // divisor for an n-bit unsigned dividend and m-bit unsigned divisor (with m ≤ n), producing an n-bit unsigned quotient. The dividend register is overwritten with the remainder on exit.

Layout (all little-endian): - dividend_qubits (n bits) → on exit: low m bits hold the remainder; high n - m bits return to |0⟩. - divisor_qubits (m bits) → preserved. - quotient_qubits (n bits) → |0⟩ on entry; quotient on exit. - work_qubits (m bits) → |0⟩ on entry and exit (high zero-pad of R). - divisor_pad_qubit (1 bit) → ancilla, |0⟩ on entry and exit. - c_qubits → carry-scratch, width ≥ (n + 1) (m + 2): first (m + 2) qubits are the shared clean comparator slice; remaining n × (m + 2) are dirty per-iteration slices for the conditional subtracts. - div_zero_flag (1 bit) → set to 1 iff divisor == 0.

For the square case n = m = q this reduces exactly to :func:q_div_restoring; the square version is kept as a convenience name and points to its own dedicated implementation rather than delegating, to avoid spurious widening of the q_div alias.

Cost: n iterations × (q_sub + q_sub_inv + q_sub_ctrl) each of width m + 1 ⇒ O(n m) Toffolis. Ancilla: (n + 1)(m + 2) carry + m work + 1 divisor-pad + 1 div-zero-flag.

Use this for Class A (|num| / den at GP fractional precision) and Class C (post-affine /(R_ox − R_red)) where the dividend has been pre-scaled (bit-shifted left by q_frac) to give fractional output.

docs.title: q_div_restoring_inv
docs.text:
q_div_restoring_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, dividend_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_qubits: Sequence[int], quotient_qubits: Sequence[int], work_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_pad_qubit: int, c_qubits: Sequence[int], div_zero_flag: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Exact inverse of :func:q_div_restoring.

Restores all registers to their state immediately before the matching :func:q_div_restoring call: - dividend_qubits returns from holding the remainder back to the original dividend value. - quotient_qubits returns to |0⟩. - work_qubits was already |0⟩ after the forward call; it stays |0⟩. - c_qubits all returns to |0⟩ (both the comparator slice, which was clean already, and the q dirty per-iteration slices). - divisor_pad_qubit returns to |0⟩. - div_zero_flag returns to its pre-call value (|0⟩ if the forward call set it; the div-by-zero detection is self-inverse). - divisor_qubits unchanged throughout.

This is the prerequisite for QAE-style oracle composition: with the forward+inverse pair, the divider acts as a clean unitary on (dividend, divisor, quotient) with all ancilla returned to |0⟩, making it composable inside controlled-power-of-Q reflections.

docs.title: q_div_nonrestoring
docs.text:
q_div_nonrestoring(qc: QuantumCircuit, dividend_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_qubits: Sequence[int], quotient_qubits: Sequence[int], work_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_pad_qubit: int, c_qubits: Sequence[int], div_zero_flag: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Unsigned fixed-point non-restoring division (Thapliyal-style).

Drop-in replacement for :func:q_div_restoring with identical signature, identical semantics on the output registers, and ~2× fewer two-qubit gates per iteration after transpilation. Computes quotient = dividend // divisor and overwrites the dividend register with the remainder.

Algorithm: - First iteration (i = q − 1): unconditional subtract of the divisor from the running window, then copy NOT sign to quotient[q−1]. - Subsequent iterations (i = q − 2 .. 0): one controlled add-or-subtract of the divisor — subtract iff the previous quotient bit (i.e. previous NOT sign) was 1, otherwise add. Then copy NOT sign to quotient[i]. - Final correction: if the final sign is negative (i.e. quotient[0] == 0), add the divisor back so the remainder is non-negative.

The savings vs restoring come from doing one controlled add-or-subtract per iteration instead of restoring's "trial-subtract → CNOT sign → undo → conditional subtract" four-step sequence; the transpiled CX cost per iteration drops from ~58(q+1) to ~16(q+1).

Layout (identical to :func:q_div_restoring): - dividend_qubits (q) → on exit: remainder. - divisor_qubits (q) → preserved. - quotient_qubits (q) → |0⟩ on entry, quotient on exit. - work_qubits (q) → |0⟩ on entry, restored to |0⟩ on exit (high half of the conceptual 2q-bit running register R = work || dividend). - divisor_pad_qubit (1) → ancilla, |0⟩ on entry and exit; zero-pad MSB of the divisor. - c_qubits → carry-scratch, width ≥ (q + 1) * (q + 2). Layout: one fresh (q + 2)-slice per iteration (q in total) plus a final (q + 2)-slice for the correction add. - div_zero_flag (1) → set to 1 iff divisor == 0 on entry.

docs.title: q_div_nonrestoring_inv
docs.text:
q_div_nonrestoring_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, dividend_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_qubits: Sequence[int], quotient_qubits: Sequence[int], work_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_pad_qubit: int, c_qubits: Sequence[int], div_zero_flag: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Exact inverse of :func:q_div_nonrestoring.

Restores all registers to their pre-call state, including the carry register, work register, quotient (back to |0⟩), and dividend (remainder → original). Prerequisite for QAE-style oracle composition.

docs.title: synth_pixel_map
docs.text:
synth_pixel_map(qc: QuantumCircuit, in_qubits: Sequence[int], out_qubits: Sequence[int], table: Sequence[int]) -> QuantumCircuit

Write an arbitrary per-pixel map into fresh output qubits.

|x⟩|0⟩ → |x⟩|table[x]⟩ where x is the integer held by in_qubits (LSB first) and table[x] the integer written into out_qubits (LSB first). The inputs are preserved and no ancilla is used, so the circuit is garbage-free and its own inverse.

Each output bit is emitted as the fixed-polarity Reed-Muller expansion of lowest multi-controlled-X cost, the polarity being chosen by exhaustive search over the 2^{len(in_qubits)} polarities. The construction is generic in the register widths and exact at every width; its cost grows as 2^{len(in_qubits)} in the worst case, so it is a compilation device for narrow registers, not a scalable arithmetic construction.

This is the synthesis behind :func:q_div_lookup and behind the Class-A and Class-C per-pixel maps of :mod:qimp.processing.ratiometric_circuit.

docs.title: q_div_lookup
docs.text:
q_div_lookup(qc: QuantumCircuit, dividend_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_qubits: Sequence[int], quotient_qubits: Sequence[int], div_zero_flag: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Out-of-place integer divider synthesised from its truth table.

|a⟩|d⟩|0⟩|0⟩ → |a⟩|d⟩|a // d⟩|0⟩ for d > 0 and |a⟩|0⟩|0⟩|0⟩ → |a⟩|0⟩|2^q − 1⟩|1⟩ (quotient and flag convention of :func:q_div_nonrestoring). Both operands are preserved and no ancilla is used, so the circuit is garbage-free and its own inverse.

A thin wrapper over :func:synth_pixel_map. The synthesis is generic in q and exact at every width; its cost grows as 2^{2q}, so it is the cheaper divider only at small widths. At q = 2 it compiles to 48 CNOTs on 7 qubits, against 189 CNOTs on 22 qubits for :func:q_div_nonrestoring; the long-division construction takes over at q = 4 (1250 against 445).

docs.title: q_div_lookup_inv
docs.text:
q_div_lookup_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, dividend_qubits: Sequence[int], divisor_qubits: Sequence[int], quotient_qubits: Sequence[int], div_zero_flag: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Inverse of :func:q_div_lookup, which is self-inverse.

docs.title: neqr_compare_swap
docs.text:
neqr_compare_swap(qc: QuantumCircuit, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int], flag_qubit: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Reversible compare-and-swap: (a, b) ← (min(a, b), max(a, b)).

Layout (little-endian, width q unless stated): - a_qubits, b_qubits (q) → on exit: a holds the minimum, b the maximum. - c_qubits (q + 1) → carry scratch, |0⟩ on entry and on exit. - flag_qubit (1) → |0⟩ on entry; on exit holds 1 iff the inputs satisfied a > b (the registers were swapped).

Steps: :func:neqr_comparator writes a > b into the flag, the trailing :func:q_sub_inv restores b and the carry register, and one Fredkin gate per bit swaps a and b under the flag. Equal inputs are not swapped.

The flag cannot be uncomputed from the sorted outputs alone (sorting is not injective), so it is the garbage bit that keeps the map reversible. Only :func:neqr_compare_swap_inv returns it to |0⟩.

Cost: one q_sub / q_sub_inv pair (4q Toffolis) plus q Fredkin gates.

docs.title: neqr_compare_swap_inv
docs.text:
neqr_compare_swap_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, a_qubits: Sequence[int], b_qubits: Sequence[int], c_qubits: Sequence[int], flag_qubit: int) -> QuantumCircuit

Exact inverse of :func:neqr_compare_swap.

Swaps back under the flag, then recomputes the comparison on the restored inputs, which clears flag_qubit to |0⟩. The carry register is |0⟩ on entry and exit.

docs.title: neqr_sort
docs.text:
neqr_sort(qc: QuantumCircuit, registers: Sequence[Sequence[int]], c_qubits: Sequence[int], flag_qubits: Sequence[int], descending: bool = False) -> QuantumCircuit

Pairwise compare-and-swap sort of k intensity registers.

Layout (little-endian): - registers (k × q) → k registers of equal width q; on exit their values are sorted, ascending along the list (registers[0] holds the minimum) or descending if descending=True. - c_qubits (q + 1) → carry scratch shared by every comparator, |0⟩ on entry and on exit. - flag_qubits (k (k - 1) / 2) → one |0⟩ ancilla per comparator; on exit flag j records whether comparator j swapped.

Algorithm: odd-even transposition network. It runs k rounds; round r applies :func:neqr_compare_swap to the neighbouring pairs (i, i + 1) with i ≡ r (mod 2). After k rounds any input is sorted (0-1 principle). Comparators within a round act on disjoint registers but share the carry scratch, so as built they run sequentially; giving each one its own carry register would allow depth O(k q).

Reversibility: sorting is many-to-one, so the flags are kept as garbage and stay entangled with the sorted registers. The flags together with the sorted values determine the input, and :func:neqr_sort_inv uses them to restore it and clear the flags. Measuring only the sorted registers is unaffected by the flags.

Cost: k (k - 1) / 2 compare-and-swaps, i.e. 2 k (k - 1) q Toffolis plus k (k - 1) q / 2 Fredkin gates. Ancilla: q + 1 carry + k (k - 1) / 2 flags.

Like the other primitives, this acts only on the qubits passed in. The registers are separate intensity registers (for instance the intensities of k NEQR images, or k pixels already loaded into their own registers); a single NEQR state holds its pixels in one register under a position superposition, so sorting its pixels against each other is not a register-level operation.

docs.title: qimp.processing.ratiometric_circuit
docs.text:
Autonomous quantum circuits for per-pixel ratiometric image operators.

Each builder takes two NEQR-encoded intensity images and constructs a circuit that computes the ratio, normalised difference or calibrated ratio on the quantum device. No classically pre-computed target is loaded into the circuit; the per-pixel value is produced by reversible arithmetic (or by an exact synthesised pixel map in the lookup variants) acting uniformly on the position superposition.

The module provides:

  • Class B, simple integer ratio R = I_a // I_b: :func:class_b_ratio (restoring, non-restoring or lookup divider), its inverse :func:class_b_ratio_inv and the decoder :func:decode_class_b_ratio.
  • Class A, Laurdan generalised polarisation GP = (I_a - G * I_b) / (I_a + G * I_b) for a classical G > 0: the numerator/denominator stage :func:class_a_gp_prefix, the full fractional pipeline :func:class_a_gp_full, the synthesised variant :func:class_a_gp_lookup, and the decoders :func:decode_class_a_prefix and :func:decode_class_a_full. G is represented in fixed point as K / 2^f (see :func:gp_g_fixed_point); G = 1 uses the plain add/subtract path.
  • Class C, roGFP calibrated ratio R_C = (R - R_red) / (R_ox - R_red): :func:class_c_rogfp_full, :func:class_c_rogfp_lookup, the primitive :func:affine_subtract_constant and the decoder :func:decode_class_c_rogfp.
  • Shared pieces: the dual-channel NEQR loader :func:dual_neqr_load and its inverse, and the threshold marking oracle :func:mark_good_oracle and its inverse, used as building blocks for amplitude estimation or Grover search over the computed image.

Intensities are q-bit unsigned integers and the position register has 2n qubits. Registers are little-endian. Unless a builder states otherwise, carry ancillas are left dirty and the result is read out by measurement; the *_inv functions are provided where full uncomputation is needed.

dual_neqr_load(qc: QuantumCircuit, image_a: ndarray, image_b: ndarray, q: int, position_qubits: list[int], intensity_a_qubits: list[int], intensity_b_qubits: list[int], mode: str = 'mcx', compress: bool = False) -> None

Load two co-registered intensity images into NEQR registers sharing a single position register.

mode="mcx" (default) writes each set pixel bit with a multi-controlled X; mode="ucry" writes each bit-plane with one uniformly controlled Ry (2^(2n) CNOTs per plane), which is far cheaper from n = 2 upward.

The position register is placed into uniform superposition via H on every position qubit. For each pixel (row, col) with non-zero intensity, controlled-X gates write the intensity into the intensity registers conditioned on the position pattern.

docs.title: dual_neqr_load_inv
docs.text:
dual_neqr_load_inv(qc: QuantumCircuit, image_a: ndarray, image_b: ndarray, q: int, position_qubits: list[int], intensity_a_qubits: list[int], intensity_b_qubits: list[int], mode: str = 'mcx', compress: bool = False) -> None

Inverse of :func:dual_neqr_load.

Each per-pixel X-MCX-X block in the forward call is self-inverse, so re-applying it cancels the original encoding. The final Hadamard on the position register is also self-inverse. To match the forward's gate ORDER reversed:

forward: H(position) → encode pixel 0 → encode pixel 1 → … → encode pixel N inverse: encode pixel N → encode pixel N-1 → … → encode pixel 0 → H(position)

Since per-pixel encodings commute (they leave the position register invariant between pixels and act on disjoint intensity-bit combinations), the iteration order can match the forward's exactly; we still walk it in the same row-major order for stylistic consistency. The H is moved to the END of the body.

class_b_ratio(image_a: ndarray, image_b: ndarray, q: int, divider: str = 'restoring', load: str = 'mcx') -> tuple[QuantumCircuit, dict[str, list[int] | int]]

Build an autonomous Class-B integer-quotient ratio circuit.

For each pixel position p in superposition, the circuit computes R(p) = I_a(p) // I_b(p) using reversible division (no classical pre-computation of R).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default image_a ndarray

2D arrays of the two intensity channels (shape 2^n × 2^n).

required image_b ndarray

2D arrays of the two intensity channels (shape 2^n × 2^n).

required q int

Width of each intensity register, in qubits.

required divider str

"restoring" (default, historical) or "nonrestoring" (Thapliyal-style; ~50% fewer two-qubit gates after transpile, same output semantics, same ancilla footprint).

'restoring'

Returns:

Type Description (qc, layout)

qc is the assembled QuantumCircuit layout is a dict with qubit-index lists for each named register: position, I_a, I_b, quotient, work, pad, c, flag.

Notes

The quotient is read out by measuring the quotient register. The flag qubit is set to 1 for pixels where I_b == 0 (the quotient at those pixels is undefined and the caller must mask them in the decoded image).

Resource costs:

  • Qubits: 2n + 4q + 2 + (q+1)(q+2). At n=1, q=2: 24 qubits.
  • Toffolis: O(q²) for the division, once for all pixel branches (the division acts uniformly on the position superposition).

docs.title: class_a_gp_lookup
docs.text:
class_a_gp_lookup(image_a: ndarray, image_b: ndarray, q: int, q_frac: int = 2, load: str = 'ucry', G: float = 1.0, g_frac_bits: int | None = None) -> tuple[QuantumCircuit, dict[str, list[int] | int]]

Class-A Laurdan GP circuit whose per-pixel map is synthesised.

Same observable and same read-out convention as :func:class_a_gp_full. With A = 2^f I_a and B = K I_b (G_eff = K / 2^f from :func:gp_g_fixed_point; A = I_a, B = I_b for G = 1),

magnitude(p) = floor(|A(p) - B(p)| * 2^q_frac / (A(p) + B(p)))
sign(p)      = 1  iff  B(p) > A(p)
div_flag(p)  = 1  iff  I_a(p) + I_b(p) = 0

so :func:decode_class_a_full decodes it unchanged. The arithmetic cascade of :func:class_a_gp_full (multiply, subtract, absolute value, shift, divide) is replaced by one :func:synth_pixel_map over the two intensity registers. Both operands are preserved and no ancilla is used: 2n + 2q + q_frac + 3 qubits for every G, against 71 for the arithmetic pipeline at n = 1, q = 2, q_frac = 2, G = 1. G only changes the synthesised table, not the qubit count. The synthesis is generic in q and exact, and its cost grows as 2^{2q}.

Layout keys: position, I_a, I_b, quotient (magnitude, q_frac + 1 bits), sign, div_flag.

docs.title: class_c_rogfp_lookup
docs.text:
class_c_rogfp_lookup(image_a: ndarray, image_b: ndarray, q: int, q_frac: int, R_red_fp: int, load: str = 'ucry') -> tuple[QuantumCircuit, dict[str, list[int] | int]]

Class-C roGFP circuit whose per-pixel map is synthesised.

Same observable and same read-out convention as :func:class_c_rogfp_full,

ratio(p)     = floor(I_a(p) · 2^q_frac / I_b(p))
rc_signed(p) = ratio(p) − R_red_fp        (two's complement)
div_flag(p)  = 1  iff  I_b(p) = 0

so :func:decode_class_c_rogfp decodes it unchanged. At I_b = 0 the fixed-point ratio takes the all-ones convention of the library's divider before the subtraction. The cascade of :func:class_c_rogfp_full is replaced by one :func:synth_pixel_map; 2n + 2q + (q + q_frac + 1) + 1 qubits against 114 at n = 1, q = q_frac = 4.

Layout keys: position, I_a, I_b, rc_signed, div_flag.

docs.title: mark_good_oracle
docs.text:
mark_good_oracle(qc: QuantumCircuit, value_qubits: list[int], threshold: int, good_qubit: int, threshold_reg_qubits: list[int], sub_carry_qubits: list[int], value_pad_qubit: int) -> None

Flip good_qubit iff value > threshold.

Implementation: build a (q+1)-bit value_padded register by appending a zero-pad ancilla to the q-bit value, materialise threshold + 1 into a (q+1)-bit constant register, and subtract threshold_reg ← threshold_reg − value_padded. The no-borrow bit of the result is 1 iff threshold + 1 ≥ value, i.e. value ≤ threshold CNOT that into good_qubit and then X-flip it so good_qubit ^= (value > threshold). Uncompute the subtract and the constant materialisation so all ancilla return to |0⟩.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default value_qubits list[int]

q-bit unsigned register holding the value to test. Preserved.

required threshold int

Classical integer in [0, 2^q − 1]. The predicate value > threshold is checked.

required good_qubit int

Single qubit XORed with the predicate's truth value.

required threshold_reg_qubits list[int]

q + 1-bit ancilla, |0⟩ on entry and exit. Holds threshold + 1 during the test.

required sub_carry_qubits list[int]

q + 2-bit carry register for the (q+1)-wide subtract, |0⟩ on entry and exit.

required value_pad_qubit int

Single ancilla, |0⟩ on entry and exit. Used as the high zero-pad of value to widen it from q to q+1 bits for the subtract.

required Notes

The construction is its own inverse: applying it twice on the same inputs returns good_qubit to its initial state (two XORs cancel), and all ancillas are restored each call. See :func:mark_good_oracle_inv for the symmetric API.

gp_g_fixed_point(G: float, g_frac_bits: int | None = None) -> tuple[int, int]

Fixed-point representation G_eff = K / 2^f used by the Class-A builders.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default G float

GP G-factor; must be finite and strictly positive.

required g_frac_bits int | None

Number of fractional bits f. None (default) selects the smallest f in [0, 16] for which G * 2^f is an integer, so dyadic values (1.0, 0.5, 1.25, 2.0, ...) are represented exactly. A non-dyadic G (e.g. 0.94) needs an explicit g_frac_bits; it is then rounded to round(G * 2^f) / 2^f.

None

Returns:

Type Description (K, f)

The integer multiplier and the number of fractional bits, so that G_eff = K / 2**f.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If G is not finite and positive, if g_frac_bits is negative, if g_frac_bits is None and G is not dyadic within 16 bits, or if round(G * 2^f) is 0 (G too small for the chosen f).

docs.title: class_a_gp_prefix
docs.text:
class_a_gp_prefix(image_a: ndarray, image_b: ndarray, q: int, G: float = 1.0, g_frac_bits: int | None = None) -> tuple[QuantumCircuit, dict[str, list[int] | int]]

Class A GP prefix stage: numerator and denominator registers.

Computes, per pixel in superposition, with G_eff = K / 2^f from :func:gp_g_fixed_point,

num(p) = 2^f I_a(p) - K I_b(p)   (two's complement, L + 1 bits)
den(p) = 2^f I_a(p) + K I_b(p)   (unsigned, L + 1 bits)

so that num / den = (I_a - G_eff I_b) / (I_a + G_eff I_b). For G_eff = 1 this is num = I_a - I_b, den = I_a + I_b with L = q. The full pipeline :func:class_a_gp_full continues from these registers (absolute value, shift, divide); the prefix alone is small enough to verify bit-exactly at small (n, q).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default image_a ndarray

Square 2^n x 2^n integer images with values in [0, 2^q - 1].

required image_b ndarray

Square 2^n x 2^n integer images with values in [0, 2^q - 1].

required q int

Intensity bit width.

required G float

GP G-factor, finite and > 0. Default 1.0.

1.0 g_frac_bits int | None

Fractional bits used to represent G; see :func:gp_g_fixed_point. None picks the exact dyadic representation.

None

Returns:

Type Description (qc, layout)

The circuit and the qubit-index layout described in the notes.

Notes

Output layout (all little-endian):

  • position (2n): shared NEQR position register, in uniform superposition after dual_neqr_load.
  • I_a, I_b (q each): NEQR intensities, preserved.
  • num (L + 1): A - B two's complement, MSB = sign (1 iff A < B).
  • den (L + 1): A + B unsigned.
  • add_c, sub_c (L + 1 each): dirty carry registers.
  • Only when G_eff != 1: g_b (L) holding K * I_b, mul_c (popcount(K) (q + 2), dirty) and mul_guard (1, returned to 0).

Here L = q for G_eff = 1 and L = max(q + f, q + bit_length(K)) otherwise. Qubits: 2n + 2q + 4(L + 1), plus L + popcount(K)(q + 2) + 1 when G_eff != 1.
